idiom_name: component contract + configuration script + component repository + linker facade + lifecycle
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: publish one Component contract (uniform operations plus init/fini lifecycle hooks) in an artifact both host and component depend on, and describe the composition in an external configuration script whose directives name the component, the implementation to link (path/symbol, class name, assembly or bundle), and its parameters. A Component Configurator parses and validates the whole script before touching the running composition, resolves each referenced implementation through the platform's dynamic linking facility behind a uniform interface, instantiates the component and inserts it into a Component Repository keyed by name, then calls the lifecycle hooks in dependency order. Unlink reverses that sequence after a drain phase. The configuration file format is free (INI-style, XML, JSON, YAML, or a custom DSL) but must be parseable before any mutation to the running composition so that a half-read script cannot leave the system in an inconsistent state.
code_sketch:
# application.conf - the configuration script
# <directive> <name> <implementation/entry point> [params]
dynamic  logfile  ./lib/libfile_logger.so:file_logger_create   path=/var/log/app.log
static   timer    builtin:timer_service                         resolution=10ms
suspend  logfile            # stop dispatching to it, keep the instance
unlink   timer              # drain -> fini() -> release implementation
# configurator: parse -> validate -> repository.add(name, impl) -> impl.init()
pitfalls: Executing the configuration before validating it: a half-read or invalid script must fail without having linked anything, or the running composition is left in an unknown half-state.
Unlinking an implementation while references to it are still live somewhere (callbacks, threads, caches) - the process then crashes inside code that was already removed.
Letting the repository become a global service locator that components query at call time, which turns configuration into hidden coupling and makes unlink order unprovable.

Treating the configuration script as an operational file rather than as code: it decides which implementations execute with the host's privileges and therefore needs review, versioning and a trusted location.

Loading components from paths on the system search path instead of absolute paths: exposes the host to DLL search order hijacking, where an attacker places a malicious DLL earlier in the search path than a legitimate system library.

Classloader memory leaks in JVM-based implementations: holding any reference to a class, object, or thread-local belonging to an unloaded component's classloader prevents garbage collection of the entire classloader and its loaded classes, eventually exhausting metaspace.

Symbol collision between components: using RTLD_GLOBAL on Linux or placing multiple components in the same classloader namespace exposes components to symbol interposition where one component's symbols override another's, producing silent wrong behaviour at runtime.

Wrong move: assuming dlclose() (or any equivalent unload API) actually removes the code -> failure: glibc keeps the object mapped when another loaded object still binds its symbols, when it registered thread-local storage destructors, or when it was linked with -z nodelete or contains STB_GNU_UNIQUE symbols, so a 'fixed' component reloaded after a hot swap silently reuses the old code -> instead: treat unload as best-effort, verify it actually happened (LD_DEBUG, /proc/self/maps), and design for replace-by-process-restart whenever true removal is a hard requirement.

Wrong move: letting a component ship its own copy of the contract library -> failure: the loader keeps two distinct copies of the same type and its globals alive in one process (dlopen treats different paths as different objects; separate JVM classloaders and .NET load contexts behave the same way), so casts fail, hooks register against the wrong registry and state silently diverges -> instead: resolve the contract exactly once in the host and delegate parent-first (shared interface classloader, host-owned AssemblyLoadContext, contract symbols exported only by the executable), and verify the contract version at link time.

Wrong move: continuing to serve after a required component fails to load -> failure: as in Envoy's remote dynamic-module fetch in fail-open mode, the filter chain simply omits the missing filter and traffic passes through without the intended policy, or with classloader retention the old component keeps serving under the new configuration's name -> instead: make a missing or unloadable required component fail closed - PostgreSQL refuses to start at all when a shared_preload_libraries entry cannot be found - or NACK the configuration until the component loads.
